narrative:
The model estimates a 74% chance that you will leave, which is high enough that the promotion decision treats you as a retention risk and therefore denies the promotion. This is not a judgment of your competence; it means your work-history pattern resembles employees who exit more than employees who stay.

The strongest signal increasing that risk was your total work experience. At 6–10 years, you are in a less common group among employees predicted to stay, most of whom have 1–5 years total experience, and this longer record appears to make leaving more likely in the model. The second-strongest signal was your time in your current organization, also 1–5 years, which further pushed the prediction toward leaving. Together, these experience patterns suggest a profile with enough accumulated experience to be mobile. The main factor pulling you toward staying was that you reported no other job opportunities; most employees predicted to stay also had none, so this lowered the risk, but not enough to offset the experience signals.

Next, you and your organization should discuss concrete retention and development steps: clarify promotion criteria and timing, review recognition, pay satisfaction, job stability, and stress or workload concerns, and agree on a career path. The organization should treat this as a retention warning rather than a final judgment, and you should ask what would change the prediction and support a future promotion.
